topicTitle: Modern Build Tools & Bundlers (Vite, ESBuild, Babel)

lessons.title: Asset Bundling Principles & Dev Server HMR via Vite
lessons.description: Bundlers combine your code into optimized files — Vite does this with lightning-fast HMR for instant feedback.

sections.heading: Why bundlers?
paragraphs: Browsers can't efficiently load hundreds of separate JavaScript files. Bundlers combine them into optimized files, transforming modern syntax and handling dependencies.
list: Combine many files into one or a few optimized bundles
Transform modern syntax for browser compatibility
Handle CSS, images, fonts and other assets
HMR (Hot Module Replacement) updates code without page reload

codeExamples.heading: Vite basics
explanation: Vite uses native ES modules in development — no bundling needed.
HMR updates changed modules instantly without page reload.
For production, Vite uses Rollup to create optimized bundles.
Vite is significantly faster than webpack for development.

practice.task: Create a Vite project, add a JavaScript module, and verify that HMR updates the page instantly when you change the module.
hints: Edit a module and observe the instant update.

keyTakeaways: Bundlers combine many files into optimized bundles for the browser.
Vite uses native ES modules in dev for instant startup.
HMR updates code without page reload — essential for fast development.
Production builds use Rollup for optimized, minified output.
lessons.challenge: Configure Vite with TypeScript, CSS modules and a custom build target.

lessons.title: AST Transformations & Polyfills via Babel
lessons.description: Babel transforms modern JavaScript into older syntax that all browsers can run.

sections.heading: What does Babel do?
list: Transforms modern syntax (arrow functions, classes) to ES5
Adds polyfills for missing APIs (Promise, Array.from, etc.)
Works as a build step or runtime transform

codeExamples.heading: Babel transformation
explanation: Babel converts arrow functions to regular functions for older browsers.
@babel/preset-env automatically determines which transforms are needed.

practice.task: Install Babel and configure it to compile a modern JavaScript file to ES5. Compare the input and output.

keyTakeaways: Babel transforms modern JavaScript into compatible syntax for older browsers.
Polyfills add missing APIs for older environments.
Most modern bundlers include Babel or equivalent transforms by default.
lessons.challenge: Configure Babel to only transform syntax needed for browsers with >1% market share.

lessons.title: Code Minification, Tree-Shaking & Source Map Generation
lessons.description: Optimize production bundles with minification, tree-shaking dead code and source maps for debugging.

sections.heading: Production optimizations
list: Minification — removes whitespace, shortens variable names, reduces file size
Tree-shaking — removes unused code from the bundle
Source maps — map minified code back to original source for debugging
All modern bundlers support these optimizations

codeExamples.heading: Optimization in practice
explanation: Minification removes all unnecessary characters — dramatic size reduction.
Tree-shaking analyzes imports and removes unused exports.
Source maps let you debug the original code in DevTools.
Vite and webpack do all of these by default for production builds.

practice.task: Build a project with Vite, check the bundle size before and after minification, and verify tree-shaking removes unused imports.
hints: Run npm run build and check the dist/ folder.
Import only 1 of 5 functions from a module.
Verify the unused functions are not in the bundle.

keyTakeaways: Minification removes whitespace and shortens names — reduces file size.
Tree-shaking removes unused code — only import what you use.
Source maps let you debug original code in production.
Modern bundlers do all of this automatically for production builds.
lessons.challenge: Compare bundle sizes with and without tree-shaking for a project that imports a large library.
